name: Skinmaxxing

lead: Skinmaxxing is the community word for working on skin so the face looks clearer, smoother and more even. Skin sits on the face in plain view, so forum members treat it as one of the most visible parts of overall appearance, alongside bone structure and hair.

The approach ranges from a basic routine (cleanser, moisturiser, sunscreen) to acne treatment, red or dark marks left after acne, scar procedures and diet. Dermatology guidance on the basics is well established, while the more elaborate stacks and procedure plans shared online vary widely in how much research stands behind them.

paras: Members typically start with a gentle cleanse, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, then add targeted actives for acne, texture or marks, and sometimes clinical procedures such as light-based treatments or subcision for scars. Threads describe building a routine over months, tracking how the skin responds, and combining it with diet and sleep changes.

Harsh soaps, over-exfoliation and piling on many actives are described in dermatology references as ways to irritate the skin barrier, and leave-on products can contain fragrances or preservatives that cause allergies. Prescription treatments and in-office procedures carry their own side-effect profiles and are generally decided with a clinician.

angle.text: Skinmaxxing works on the face's surface directly: reducing active breakouts, fading the marks they leave and improving texture and tone. Members describe the payoff as a cleaner, more even complexion that reads as healthier in photos and in person.

lead: Skinmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for deliberately improving the look and condition of one's skin. It spans everything from a first cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen routine to long multi-step plans covering acne, post-acne red or brown marks, texture, scarring and radiance (often called 'glow' or 'glass skin') [1][2][3].

The reasoning behind it is that skin is the surface on which every other facial feature is read: a clearer, more even complexion changes how a whole face looks without altering its structure. Members of looksmax.org describe it as the most common topic on the forum and as a lever that costs less and carries less risk than surgery, while some pair it with clinical procedures [2]. Looksmaxxing is usually divided into 'softmaxxing' (non-invasive changes such as skincare, grooming and fitness) and 'hardmaxxing' (medical or invasive routes), and skincare is the standard example of the former [3].

The practice rests on a base of well-documented dermatology: cleansing to remove oil and dirt, moisturising to hydrate and support the barrier, and sunscreen to limit UV damage and photoageing [4][5]. Forum guides add actives such as retinoids and acids, light-based treatments, dietary changes and supplements, written largely from individual members' experience [6][2]. The American Academy of Dermatology has published a clinical page on looksmaxxing that lists skin complications dermatologists may see from trend-driven practices [7].

paras: Skinmaxxing covers any deliberate effort to improve skin quality for appearance. In forum usage it tends to have three layers: a maintenance routine, targeted treatment of a specific concern, and optional procedures [1][6][2]. The goals named most often are clarity (fewer breakouts), evenness (fading of red and brown marks), smoothness (texture and scars), oil balance and an overall radiant or 'glass' finish [2][8].

General skin-care references describe the routine layer. Cleansers remove oil, dirt and makeup; synthetic-detergent cleansers sit closer to neutral pH than traditional alkaline soaps and are generally recommended for people with skin conditions; moisturisers raise the skin's water content and may support the barrier with regular use; and sunscreen guards against UV damage [4]. Dermatological consensus, as summarised there, puts gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection first [4].

The wider looksmaxxing vocabulary emerged on message boards in the 2010s, and the practice moved to TikTok in the early 2020s, where much early content was framed as self-improvement [3]. Skincare has a longer pedigree in men's magazines such as GQ, Esquire and Men's Health, which carried grooming and skin advice before the term existed [3].

Skinmaxxing draws on several adjacent traditions. Korean beauty culture popularised long multi-step routines and the 'glass skin' ideal of a luminous, even complexion, and its routines typically run through a double cleanse, essences, serums and moisturiser, ending with sunscreen by day [9]. Dermatology-led acne and photoageing treatments (retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid, light and laser devices) supply much of the active-ingredient and procedure vocabulary [10][11][12]. Forum posters then collect these into guides; a looksmax.org thread invites members to post 'the best skinmaxxing guides' they know, and other threads are devoted to single topics such as matte versus radiant finish, blue-light exposure and glutathione [13][8][14][15].

Descriptions of the practice in forums and in general references can be grouped into a handful of components. The details below are general; individual products and regimens vary and are chosen with a clinician when medical treatments are involved.

Forum questions often begin here. In one thread a member who found that sensitive-skin cleansers left the face red asks for recommendations, and a reply attributes the redness to a damaged skin barrier and suggests cleansing at night only, a mineral sunscreen in the morning and moisturiser twice daily [1]. Skin-care references note that over-washing does not cause oil overproduction but can cause dryness, and that moisturising twice daily may strengthen the barrier in sensitive skin [4].

Sunscreen is the most consistently cited element. Sunscreen reduces the UV exposure that causes sunburn, premature ageing and skin cancer, and it is also advised to stop post-acne marks from darkening [5][10]. A 2013 Australian study of about 900 people reported that daily broad-spectrum use over four and a half years left skin smoother and more resilient than usual habits, and a smaller study reported improved photoageing signs after 12 weeks of daily SPF 30 [5]. Mineral filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) are the ones the US classes as generally recognised as safe and effective, and forum posters often recommend them for reactive skin [5][1].

subs.h: Actives for acne, texture and tone
paras: Topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide are first-line acne treatments in dermatology, and retinoids also help fade post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; azelaic acid and salicylic acid are other options [10]. Retinoids are also used for photoageing [11]. Dermatologists cited in skin-care references note that harsh soaps, over-exfoliation and benzoyl peroxide can dry or irritate the skin, so many routines introduce actives gradually [4]. Oral isotretinoin is the most effective oral acne option and is reserved for severe or stubborn cases, with strict pregnancy-prevention rules [10]; a forum reader of the cystic-acne guide asks whether a low dose helps with persistent red marks [6].

Skinmaxxing guides frequently include an 'internal' layer [2]. Skin-care references report that high-glycaemic diets are linked with greater sebum production and acne severity and that dairy has been linked with increased sebum, while evidence tying chocolate or salt to acne is lacking [4][10]. They also note that sleep deprivation can worsen eczema and other inflammatory skin conditions [4]. Forum threads on supplements such as glutathione reflect individual members' experiences [15].

Members also discuss in-office options. Intense pulsed light (IPL), invented by Shimon Eckhouse in 1992 and cleared by the FDA for vascular lesions in 1995 and pigmented lesions in 1996, uses filtered broad-spectrum light that targets haemoglobin in small blood vessels or melanin, and is used for redness, pigment and some acne [12]. Atrophic scars, the most common acne scar type (ice-pick, boxcar and rolling), are the target of procedures such as subcision, which one looksmax.org thread advocates for members with scarring [16][17]. Dermatology references describe light and laser therapies for acne as adjuncts with limited evidence and considerable cost [10].

Skinmaxxing threads are among the most frequent on looksmax.org. Posts range from beginner routine questions to guides written like manuals. One covers recovery from cystic acne and post-inflammatory erythema (PIE, red marks left after inflamed spots), argues that PIE is vascular rather than pigment-related, prefers IPL, and notes that the author used an AI assistant to help write the post [6]. Another, built around 'porcelain aesthetics', has sections on an internal supplement stack, topical regimens adjusted by Fitzpatrick skin type, clinical procedures, scar reversal and 'glowmaxxing' [2]. Replies to such posts range from requests for personal advice to short endorsements, with 'glass skin' described as admirable in the community's slang [2].

A recurring genre is the before-and-after claim of fast results; a thread title promises that almost all of a member's acne cleared in two days, which is an individual's report [18]. Common themes are acne control, fading marks, scar procedures, oil control versus radiance and diet [2][8]. Members often describe skin as the most changeable part of the face and the easiest place to see progress [2].

General looksmaxxing coverage in the BBC, The Guardian, The New York Times, NPR, Business Insider, GQ and Esquire, among others, treats skincare as the mild end of the spectrum, with attention concentrated on more extreme practices [3]. The American Academy of Dermatology page lists complications clinicians may see from trend-driven practices, including inflammatory reactions, foreign-body granulomas, acneiform eruptions, pigmentary changes, barrier disruption and dermatitis, and notes that patients may not regard their practices as medical [7]. It also highlights psychosocial concerns, linking appearance-focused online content to body dysmorphic disorder and anxiety, and recommends supportive counselling and referral where distress is disproportionate [7]. Its evidence base includes a March 2026 structured review of 150 TikTok videos and their comments [7].

Dermatologists quoted in general references prioritise gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection as the foundation of a routine, and recommend consulting a dermatologist for persistent or severe conditions, who can prescribe medication and customised treatments [4]. Those references describe anti-ageing products as often marketed with claims that have not been proven, note that terms like 'mild' or 'gentle' on labels are vague, and note the US Federal Trade Commission's position that nothing purchasable has been proven to reverse ageing [4].

Specific forum techniques, such as IPL for post-acne redness or particular supplement stacks, are described in the community as personal experience and are not individually assessed by published trials of skinmaxxing as a whole.

Skin-care references list over-exfoliation as a cause of irritation and barrier damage, harsh soaps and benzoyl peroxide as drying, and serums and leave-on products as possible sources of allergy through fragrances or preservatives [4]. Forum members themselves report that products meant to be gentle left their skin red and discuss barrier damage as the cause [1]. Retinoids are not recommended in pregnancy by the AAD, and oral retinoids carry specific pregnancy-prevention requirements [11][10]. IPL carries a risk of hyperpigmentation and is not suitable for every skin tone or for people on photosensitising medicines [12]. Dermatology bodies also flag appearance-focused online communities as a possible contributor to body dysmorphia and anxiety [7].

No studies found on skinmaxxing as a combined practice. Individual components are studied separately in dermatology: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen and photoageing [5], topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide in acne [10], retinoids in photoageing [11] and IPL for vascular and pigmented lesions [12]. Their evidence bases are described on the pages for those treatments.

timeline.event: The sun protection factor (SPF) system for rating sunscreens is introduced [5].
Shimon Eckhouse invents intense pulsed light, later used for redness and pigment [12].
The FDA approves IPL for vascular lesions, followed by pigmented lesions (1996) and hair removal (1997) [12].
Looksmaxxing vocabulary develops on message boards, with skincare placed under 'softmaxxing' [3].
Looksmaxxing and skincare content spreads to TikTok, often framed as self-improvement [3].
Long skinmaxxing guides covering PIE, IPL, Fitzpatrick-adjusted regimens and glowmaxxing are posted on looksmax.org [6][2].
The American Academy of Dermatology publishes a clinical page on looksmaxxing and dermatologic complications [7].
